lines.speaker: Διογένης
lines.text: Is that Heracles? By Heracles, it is. The bow, the club, the lionskin, the sheer size of the man—it's Heracles all over. So, he died, did he, even though he's the son of Zeus? Tell me, O Glorious Victor, are you actually dead? Because I used to sacrifice to you up on earth as a god.

lines.speaker: Ἡρακλῆς
lines.text: And you were quite right to do so. Heracles himself is in heaven, keeping company with the gods and married to neat-ankled Hebe. I am his phantom.

lines.speaker: Διογένης
lines.text: I'm sorry, what? The phantom of the god? Is it possible to be a god by halves, and dead by halves?

lines.speaker: Ἡρακλῆς
lines.text: Yes. He did not die. I, his image, did.

lines.speaker: Διογένης
lines.text: I see. He handed you over to Pluto as a substitute, and now you’re dead in his place.

lines.speaker: Ἡρακλῆς
lines.text: Something like that.

lines.speaker: Διογένης
lines.text: Then how did Aeacus, who’s usually such a stickler for procedure, fail to notice you weren’t him? He just accepted a counterfeit Heracles at the gate?

lines.speaker: Ἡρακλῆς
lines.text: Because I looked exactly like him.

lines.speaker: Διογένης
lines.text: Fair point. Exactly like him. As in, actually him. Watch out it isn’t the other way around: you’re the real Heracles, and it’s the phantom who’s up there with the gods, married to Hebe.

lines.speaker: Ἡρακλῆς
lines.text: You are insolent and you talk too much. If you don't stop mocking me, you'll soon find out exactly whose phantom I am.

lines.speaker: Διογένης
lines.text: [laughs] Ah, the bow is out and ready. But what do I have to fear from you? I'm already dead. Tell me though, by your Heracles—when he was alive, were you tagging along with him as a phantom even then? Or were you one person in life, and when you died, you split in two? He flew off to the gods, and you, the phantom, naturally came down to Hades?

lines.speaker: Ἡρακλῆς
lines.text: I shouldn't even answer a man who mocks me like this. But listen: whatever part of Heracles came from Amphitryon, that part died, and I am the entirety of it. But the part that came from Zeus is in heaven, consorting with the gods.

lines.speaker: Διογένης
lines.text: Ah, now I understand perfectly! You're saying Alcmene gave birth to two Heracleses at the same time: one by Amphitryon, and one by Zeus. You were secret twins, with the same mother!

lines.speaker: Ἡρακλῆς
lines.text: No, you fool! We were both the same person.

lines.speaker: Διογένης
lines.text: That's not easy to grasp. Two Heracleses spliced together? Unless you were grown into one, like a centaur—half-man, half-god.

lines.speaker: Ἡρακλῆς
lines.text: Doesn't it seem to you that everyone is composed of two things: soul and body? So what prevents the soul—which came from Zeus—from being in heaven, while the mortal part—me—is here among the dead?

lines.speaker: Διογένης
lines.text: My excellent son of Amphitryon, that would be a fine argument if you were a body. But as it is, you're an incorporeal phantom. You're in serious danger of turning Heracles into a trinity.

lines.speaker: Ἡρακλῆς
lines.text: A trinity? How?

lines.speaker: Διογένης
lines.text: Well, let's see. If one part is in heaven, and you—the phantom—are here with us, and your body has dissolved into dust... that makes three. Think about it: who are you going to invent as a third father for the body?

lines.speaker: Ἡρακλῆς
lines.text: You are an arrogant sophist! Who are you, anyway?

lines.speaker: Διογένης
lines.text: The phantom of Diogenes of Sinope. Though I myself, by Zeus, am not "with the immortal gods"—I am right here, keeping company with the best of the dead, laughing at Homer and all this miserable metaphysical nonsense.
